knowledge_graph.title: Neurofibromatosis type I
knowledge_graph.description: Neurofibromatosis type I, or von Recklinghausen syndrome, is a complex multi-system neurocutaneous disorder caused by a subset of genetic mutations at the neurofibromin 1 locus. Other conditions associated with mutation of the NF1 gene include Watson syndrome.
knowledge_graph.other_names: von Recklinghausen disease; morbus Recklinghausen; NF1

related_questions.question: What is the life expectancy of a person with NF1?
related_questions.snippet: If there are no complications, the life expectancy of people with NF1 is almost normal. With the right education, people with NF1 can live a normal life. Although mental impairment is generally mild, NF1 is a known cause of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder.

related_questions.question: At what age is neurofibromatosis diagnosed?

text_blocks.snippet: Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) is often diagnosed in childhood, with many symptoms appearing by age 10. However, diagnosis can also occur in adulthood, as some symptoms, like neurofibromas, may not appear until later in life. Neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2) is typically diagnosed in the late teens or early twenties, though some individuals may not experience symptoms until later in life.
snippet_highlighted_words: Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) is often diagnosed in childhood, with many symptoms appearing by age 10

list.title: Early Childhood:
list.snippet: Symptoms like café-au-lait spots and freckling in the armpits or groin can appear at birth or within the first few years of life.

list.title: Later Childhood:
list.snippet: Other features, such as Lisch nodules (spots on the iris) and neurofibromas (tumors on or under the skin), often emerge during childhood and adolescence.

list.title: Diagnosis:
list.snippet: NF1 is typically diagnosed based on the presence of specific clinical features, such as six or more café-au-lait spots, freckling in the armpits or groin, neurofibromas, and Lisch nodules. In some cases, genetic testing may be used to confirm the diagnosis, especially if the clinical presentation is unclear.

list.title: Mean Age of Diagnosis:
list.snippet: While symptoms can appear early, the mean age of diagnosis for NF1 is between 2.65 and 4.5 years in the absence of a family history.

list.title: Late Teens/Early Twenties:
list.snippet: Most individuals with NF2 are diagnosed in their late teens or early twenties due to the development of vestibular schwannomas (tumors on the hearing and balance nerves).

list.title: Later Onset:
list.snippet: Some individuals with NF2 may not experience noticeable symptoms until later in life, even into their 40s or later.

list.title: Diagnosis:
list.snippet: NF2 is often diagnosed based on the presence of bilateral vestibular schwannomas, along with other potential symptoms like hearing loss, tinnitus, and balance problems.

list.title: Family History:
list.snippet: Individuals with a family history of NF1 are often diagnosed earlier due to increased awareness and monitoring.

list.title: Severity of Symptoms:
list.snippet: The age of diagnosis can vary depending on the severity and number of symptoms present.

list.title: Access to Healthcare:
list.snippet: Access to specialists and genetic counseling can also influence the age at which a diagnosis is made.

text_blocks.snippet: In summary, while NF1 is often diagnosed in childhood, and NF2 in the late teens or early twenties, the age of diagnosis can vary widely depending on the specific type of neurofibromatosis, the severity of symptoms, and individual circumstances.

text_blocks.snippet: Neurofibromatosis (NF) is a genetic disorder that can cause tumors to grow along nerves in the body. The most common types, NF1 and NF2, have distinct appearances. NF1 often presents with skin changes like café-au-lait spots and freckling, as well as neurofibromas (small, benign tumors on or under the skin). NF2 is characterized by tumors on the auditory nerves, leading to hearing loss, and tumors on the brain and spinal cord.
snippet_highlighted_words: skin changes like café-au-lait spots and freckling, as well as neurofibromas (small, benign tumors on or under the skin)

list.snippet: Café-au-lait spots: Light brown patches on the skin, often larger than freckles.
Freckling: Clusters of small brown spots, usually in the armpits or groin.
Neurofibromas: Small, soft bumps on or under the skin, often appearing as pea-sized lumps.
Lisch nodules: Tiny, non-cancerous bumps on the iris (colored part of the eye).
Skeletal abnormalities: Curved spine (scoliosis), bowing of the legs, and other bone problems.
Larger than average head size .
Learning disabilities .
Hearing loss: Gradual or sudden hearing loss due to tumors on the auditory nerves.
Balance problems: May occur due to tumors affecting balance and coordination.
Facial weakness or numbness: Can be a symptom of tumors affecting facial nerves.
Tumors on the brain and spinal cord: These can cause various neurological symptoms depending on their location.
NF1 symptoms can vary widely in severity, with some individuals experiencing mild symptoms and others experiencing more significant issues.
NF2 is less common than NF1 and tends to have fewer visible signs, with symptoms often not appearing until the late teens or early twenties.
In both types, tumors can be benign (non-cancerous) or malignant (cancerous).
Regular check-ups with a healthcare professional are crucial for monitoring and managing symptoms, especially for individuals with a family history of NF.

related_questions.question: What is the Von Recklinghausen disease?
related_questions.snippet: Neurofibromatosis 1 (NF1), historically called von Recklinghausen's disease, is a genetic disorder characterized by increased risk of developing noncancerous (benign) and cancerous (malignant) tumors, as well as various other physical and neurological manifestations.
related_questions.title: Neurofibromatosis 1 - Symptoms, Causes, Treatment | NORD

text_blocks.snippet: Recklinghausen's disease is another name for Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1), a genetic disorder that causes tumors to grow on nerves throughout the body. These tumors, called neurofibromas, can be benign (non-cancerous) or cancerous. NF1 can also lead to learning difficulties and growth problems in children.
snippet_highlighted_words: another name for Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1), a genetic disorder that causes tumors to grow on nerves throughout the body

list.title: Genetic basis:
list.snippet: NF1 is caused by a mutation in the NF1 gene, which is located on chromosome 17. This gene produces neurofibromin, a protein that regulates cell growth.

list.title: Tumor development:
list.snippet: The mutation in the NF1 gene leads to uncontrolled cell growth and the formation of neurofibromas.

list.title: Symptoms:
list.snippet: Symptoms vary widely but may include:
Café-au-lait spots: Light brown skin patches.
Neurofibromas: Tumors on or under the skin, or within nerves.
Learning difficulties: Including trouble with reading, math, or attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD).
Larger than average head size and short stature .
Other potential issues: Squints, reduced vision, bulging eyes, and spinal deformities like scoliosis.

list.title: Diagnosis:
list.snippet: Diagnosis is often based on the presence of characteristic symptoms, especially café-au-lait spots and neurofibromas.

list.title: Treatment:
list.snippet: Treatment focuses on managing symptoms and complications. This may involve surgery to remove tumors, radiation therapy, chemotherapy, or other approaches.

list.title: Complications:
list.snippet: Some neurofibromas can become cancerous (Malignant Peripheral Nerve Sheath Tumors or MPNSTs).

list.title: Management:
list.snippet: Regular monitoring and follow-up with specialists are important for managing NF1 and its potential complications.
